explanations.explanation: The younger son walks up and says, “Father, give me my share of the estate.” That's the whole ask. I think that's a bold thing to say to your own father, friend. And the father hears it and divides his property between his sons.

Servants do show up in this story, but he never asks to run them. He asks, “Father, give me my share of the estate.” Later he's the one hoping to be treated like a hired servant (Luke 15:19). Being in charge of them was never on his mind.

explanations.answer: A field of his own to farm
explanations.explanation: No field comes up in his request, friend. He asks for his share of the estate, plain and simple. He does end up in a field later, but it's another man's field, and he's there to feed pigs. That's a very different farm.
Not quite, baker. The father doesn't say no. The text says he divided his property between his sons. He hands over the younger son's share, just like he was asked.
That's right. The father doesn't refuse. The text says he divided his property between both sons. The younger son asked, and the younger son got it.

Squandered is the word, friend. The younger son squandered his wealth in wild living. It means the money went out fast and nothing good came back. It's the opposite of me guarding the last chocolate chip in the bowl.
Investing sounds like a plan with a spreadsheet, and this wasn't that. The text says he squandered his wealth in wild living. Nothing in the passage says he put that money to work for him.

Sharing would be a lovely thing to do with a fortune, but that's not what happened here. The text says he squandered his wealth in wild living. And when the hunger hit, no one would give him a thing (Luke 15:16).

explanations.answer: Into his fields to feed the pigs
explanations.explanation: Pigs. The man sends him into his fields to feed the pigs. A son who started with a share of the estate is now working for a stranger. I think that's a long way down from where he started.

explanations.answer: Into his vineyard to pick grapes
explanations.explanation: Grapes would be a gentler job, friend, but the text doesn't send him there. The citizen sends him into his fields to feed the pigs. No vineyard shows up in this story.

explanations.answer: Into his house to serve meals
explanations.explanation: An indoor job with a roof sounds nice, doesn't it? But the text says he's sent into the fields. His work is feeding the pigs, not serving at a table.

I wish that were how it went, friend, but it isn't. The text says he longed to fill his belly with the pods the pigs were eating, “…no one would give him a thing.” Nobody takes pity on him with a meal. He's out there on his own.
That's right. Nobody hands him a meal. The text says “…no one would give him a thing.” He's hungry enough to long for what the pigs are eating, and no one helps.

His father is who he thinks of. He says, “How many of my father’s hired servants have plenty of food, but here I am, starving to death!” Even the hired servants back home are eating well. That's when he starts turning toward home.
No uncle in this story, friend. The younger son says, “How many of my father’s hired servants have plenty of food…” His thoughts go straight to his father's place.

A neighbor never comes up. When he comes to his senses, he says, “How many of my father’s hired servants have plenty of food…” It's his father's household he remembers, and his father's servants eating well.

explanations.answer: Like one of his hired servants
explanations.explanation: That's the plan. He means to say, “Make me like one of your hired servants.” He's already decided he's no longer worthy to be called a son. I think he's trying to ask for as little as he can.

explanations.answer: Heir of all his father's land
explanations.explanation: That's aiming way too high for where his head is at, friend. He's planning to say he's no longer worthy to be called his father's son. What he wants to ask is, “Make me like one of your hired servants.”
Running the household isn't in his speech. He says he's no longer worthy to be called a son. Then he plans to ask, “Make me like one of your hired servants.”

explanations.answer: Runs to him and embraces him
explanations.explanation: He runs. The text says the father saw him while he was still in the distance, “He ran to his son, embraced him, and kissed him.” I'd run too, but on my gold base it's more of a hop. No waiting around, friend.

explanations.answer: Waits for him at the front door
explanations.explanation: No front door waiting here. The father saw his son while he was still in the distance. Then he ran to him, embraced him, and kissed him.

explanations.answer: Sends a servant out to meet him
explanations.explanation: Servants do show up in this scene, but not for this job. The father goes himself. The text says he ran to his son, embraced him, and kissed him.

Compassion is it. The text says his father saw him and “was filled with compassion.” And that's before the son says one word of his speech. The first thing the son meets is the father running toward him.
If you were braced for anger, friend, I get it. But the text says the father “was filled with compassion.” Then he runs to his son.
No doubt in this father's heart. The text says he “was filled with compassion.” There's no standing around wondering, because he runs to his son.

explanations.answer: His son was dead and is alive again
explanations.explanation: That's the reason. The father says, “For this son of mine was dead and is alive again! He was lost and is found!” Notice he doesn't mention the money or any list of conditions. The celebration is about his son being back.

explanations.answer: His son has paid back all the money
explanations.explanation: Nobody pays anybody back in this story, friend. The son's speech is about having sinned against heaven and against his father. The father's reason for the party is, “For this son of mine was dead and is alive again!”

explanations.answer: His son has promised to work harder
explanations.explanation: No promises get made. The son says he has sinned against heaven and against his father, and that he's no longer worthy to be called his son. The father's reason is, “For this son of mine was dead and is alive again!”
Not this time, baker. The older son hears the music and dancing, but he doesn't walk in. He calls one of the servants and asks what's going on. He wants to know what's happening first.
That's right. He doesn't head straight inside. He calls one of the servants and asks what was going on. He hears a party before he knows what it's for.
True. The text says, “The older son became angry and refused to go in.” He's standing outside while the party goes on without him. I think that's a tough spot for his father too.
The text is clear about this one. It says the older son “became angry and refused to go in.” So he stays outside. That's why his father has to come out to him.
Pleads is the word. The father comes out and pleaded with him. A party's going on inside, and the father leaves it to go out to his older son. He doesn't send someone else.
No deals get made on that doorstep, friend. The text says his father came out and pleaded with him. Pleading is a different thing from haggling.
You might expect an argument, but that's not the word the text uses. It says his father came out and pleaded with him. The older son is the one who answers with his complaints.
That's not what he says, friend. He says “this son of yours.” The words my brother never come out of his mouth. It's the father who later says, “this brother of yours” (Luke 15:32).
Right. The older son says, “…when this son of yours returns…” He doesn't call him my brother. The father is the one who says, “…this brother of yours was dead and is alive again…” (Luke 15:32).

explanations.answer: Everything the father has is his
explanations.explanation: That's what the father says. “Son, you are always with me… and all that is mine is yours.” Look at how he starts, with the word son. The older son was never missing out on what the father had.

explanations.answer: A feast for him is coming soon
explanations.explanation: The father doesn't promise a future feast, friend. He says, “Son, you are always with me… and all that is mine is yours.” That's a bigger answer than any single party.

explanations.answer: He can have the next fattened calf
explanations.explanation: He gets no promise about the next fattened calf. What the father says is, “Son, you are always with me… and all that is mine is yours.” That covers way more than one calf.
Brother. The father says, “…this brother of yours was dead and is alive again…” He gives the older son back the word he left out. The younger one is still his brother.

Servants are in this story, but they're not who the father means. He says, “…this brother of yours was dead and is alive again…” The servants were only the ones who told the older son what was happening.
Friends do come up, friend. The older son complains he never got a young goat to celebrate with his friends. But the father says, “…this brother of yours was dead and is alive again…”
